abstract: Patients with psoriatic disease- psoriasis (PsO), psoriatic arthritis (PsA)-and spondyloarthritis (SpA) face elevated cardiovascular (CV) risk driven by chronic systemic inflammation. We aimed to map the CV safety landscape of biological and targeted synthetic drugs (b/tsDMARDs), evaluating reported major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), intermediate metabolic markers, and surrogate indicators of vascular health. Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, we searched PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane for randomized trials and extension studies with at least 52 weeks of cumulative exposure in PsO, PsA, and SpA. Altogether, 152 unique studies (reported across 183 publications) were included (PsO: 83; PsA: 41; SpA: 28). MACE and mortality rates remained low, predominantly clustering in individuals with high baseline CV risk. In PsO, interleukin (IL)-17 and IL-23 inhibitors showed a low hard arterial event incidence; exploratory assessments noted improved endothelial function (+2.1% flow-mediated dilation, p = 0.0022) with secukinumab, which cannot be assumed to translate into clinical event reduction. In PsA and SpA, Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors exhibited infrequent MACE reporting, with sporadic adjudicated venous thromboembolism events in selected long-term extensions. Apremilast was associated with moderate weight reduction, while tofacitinib showed dose-dependent lipid increases with a stable total/high-density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio. Most evidence derived from long-term extension studies, carrying an inherent high risk of bias due to uncontrolled designs, patient attrition, and survivor selection. In conclusion, trial data document low absolute MACE rates, yet uncontrolled extension designs preclude definitive causal or comparative inferences. Given the systematic exclusion of multimorbid individuals, individualized baseline risk stratification and prospective cardiovascular-endpoint trials remain essential.
